'''David Bryant Mumford''' (born 11 June 1937) is an American [[mathematician]] known for his work in [[algebraic geometry]] and then for research into [[computer vision|vision]] and [[pattern theory]]. He won the [[Fields Medal]] and was a [[MacArthur Fellow]]. In 2010 he was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]]. He is currently a university professor emeritus in the Division of Applied Mathematics at [[Brown University]].

==Life==
Mumford was born in [[Worth, West Sussex]] in [[England]], of an English father and American mother. His father [[William Bryant Mumford]] was educated at [[Manchester Grammar School]] and took the [[Mathematical Tripos]] at [[St John's College, Cambridge]];<ref>{{cite book |last1=Great Britain Colonial |title=The Colonial Office List |date=1924 |publisher=Harrison |page=699 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=I9cZAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA699 |language=en}}</ref> as his mother Edith Emily Read had done at [[Girton College]].<ref>{{acad|id=Drage+AND+Girton|name=Edith Emily Read}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Kanner |first1=Barbara |title=Women in Context: Two Hundred Years of British Women Autobiographers, a Reference Guide and Reader |date=1997 |publisher=G.K. Hall |isbn=978-0-8161-7346-4 |page=609 |language=en}}</ref> He started an experimental school in the colonial [[Tanganyika Territory]] and at the time of his death in 1951 worked in the [[United Nations Department of Public Information]].<ref name=fml>{{citation|title=Fields Medallists' Lectures, World Scientific Series in 20th Century Mathematics, Vol 5|date=1997|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=978-9810231170|page=225|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q6eSjV-0egUC&pg=PA225}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=British UNO Director Dies |url=https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000650/19510129/001/0001 |work=Liverpool Daily Post |date=29 January 1951|page=1}}</ref> He married in 1933 Grace Schiott of [[Southport, Connecticut]], and the couple had five children.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Burckel |first1=Christian E. |title=Who's who in the United Nations |date=1951 |publisher=C.E. Burckel and Associates. |page=311|volume=1 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1pVaAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA311 |language=en}}</ref>

Mumford first went to [[Unquowa School]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Beyond the Three Bridges, around the world – Bhāvanā |journal=Bhāvanā the mathematics magazine |date=January 2021 |volume=5 |issue=1 |url=https://bhavana.org.in/beyond-the-three-bridges-around-the-world/}}</ref> He attended [[Phillips Exeter Academy]], where he received a [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]] prize for his relay-based computer project.<ref>"Autobiography of David Mumford", ''The Shaw Prize'', [https://www.shawprize.org/prizes-and-laureates/mathematical-sciences/2006/autobiography-of-david-mumford 2006]</ref><ref>David B. Mumford, "How a Computer Works", ''Radio-Electronics'', February 1955, p. [https://worldradiohistory.com/hd2/IDX-Consumer/Archive-Radio-Electronics-IDX/IDX/50s/1955/Radio-Electronics-1955-02-OCR-Page-0056.pdf 58], [https://worldradiohistory.com/hd2/IDX-Consumer/Archive-Radio-Electronics-IDX/IDX/50s/1955/Radio-Electronics-1955-02-OCR-Page-0057.pdf 59], [https://worldradiohistory.com/hd2/IDX-Consumer/Archive-Radio-Electronics-IDX/IDX/50s/1955/Radio-Electronics-1955-02-OCR-Page-0058.pdf 60]</ref>  Mumford then went to [[Harvard University]], where he became a student of [[Oscar Zariski]]. At Harvard, he became a [[Putnam Fellow]] in 1955 and 1956.<ref name="MMA">{{citation |title=Putnam Competition Individual and Team Winners |url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/putnam-competition-individual-and-team-winners |publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]] |access-date=December 10, 2021 |archive-date=12 March 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140312205244/http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/putnam-competition-individual-and-team-winners |url-status=dead }}</ref> He completed his [[PhD]] in 1961, with a thesis entitled ''Existence of the moduli scheme for curves of any genus''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy |id=18755}}</ref>

After a career at Harvard, Mumford moved to [[Brown University]] in 1996, concentrating on [[applied mathematics]].<ref>{{cite web |title=David Mumford |url=https://nationalmedals.org/laureate/david-mumford/ |website=National Science and Technology Medals Foundation}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Yau |first1=Shing-Tung |last2=Nadis |first2=Steven J. |title=The Shape of a Life |date=1 January 2019 |publisher=Yale University Press |isbn=978-0-300-23590-6 |page=256 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ih-FDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA256 |language=en}}</ref>

==Research==
===Algebraic geometry===
Mumford's work in geometry combined traditional geometric insights with contemporary algebraic techniques. 

====Moduli spaces====
{{main|Moduli of algebraic curves}}

Mumford published on [[moduli space]]s, with a theory summed up in his book ''Geometric Invariant Theory''. 

At the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1974, [[John Tate (mathematician)|John Tate]] said:

<blockquote>Mumford's major work has been a tremendously successful multi-pronged attack on problems of the existence and structure of varieties of moduli, that is, varieties whose points parametrize isomorphism classes of some type of geometric object.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lehto |first1=Olli |title=Mathematics Without Borders: A History of the International Mathematical Union |date=6 December 2012 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4612-0613-2 |page=191 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YxTSBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA191 |language=en}}</ref></blockquote>
[[File:ModularGroup-FundamentalDomain.svg|thumb|Diagram of a [[fundamental domain]] (in grey) for the [[modular group]] acting on the [[upper half-plane]], the classical picture of moduli for curves of genus 1]]
The [[moduli space of curves]] of a given [[genus of a curve|genus]] ''g'' was already considered in [[complex algebraic geometry]] during the 19th century. When ''g'' = 1 the number of moduli is 1 also, the term coming from the [[elliptic modulus]] function of the theory of [[Jacobi elliptic functions]]. [[Bernhard Riemann]] contributed the formula, when ''g'' ≥ 2, for the number of moduli, namely 3''g''−3, a consequence, in [[deformation theory]], of the [[Riemann-Roch theorem]].<ref name="Hartshorne">{{cite book |last=Hartshorne |first=Robin |authorlink=Robin Hartshorne |title=Deformation Theory |date=10 December 2009 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-1-4419-1595-5 |page=177 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bwhEX01JlXkC&pg=PA177 |language=en}}</ref>

The theory of [[abstract varieties]], as Mumford showed, can be applied to provide an [[existence theorem]] for moduli spaces of curves, over any [[algebraically closed field]]. It therefore answers the question of in what sense there is a geometric object, with an algebraic definition, that parametrizes algebraic curves, so generalizing the [[modular curve]]s, having the predicted dimension. In a summary provided by [[Jean Dieudonné]], making use of [[scheme theory]], the steps are:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dieudonné |first1=Jean |title=Panorama des mathématiques pures: le choix bourbachique |date=1977 |publisher=Gauthier-Villars |page=141 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TTtFzwEACAAJ |language=fr}}</ref>

#Construction of a certain [[closed subscheme]] ''H'' of the [[Hilbert scheme]] of the projective space of dimension ''n'' over the [[ring of integers]].
#Construction of an "orbit scheme" ''M'' of the [[projective linear group]] ''PGL<sub>n</sub>'' acting on ''H''. This step relies on the more tractable theory of [[moduli of abelian varieties]].

In the introduction to his 1965 book ''Geometric Invariant Theory'', Mumford described the construction of "moduli schemes of various types of objects" as essentially "a special and highly non-trivial case" of the problem "when does an [[orbit (group theory)|orbit]] space of an [[algebraic scheme]] acted on by an [[algebraic group]] exist?". For this area, see [[algebraic invariant theory]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mumford |first1=David |title=Geometric Invariant Theory |date=1965 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=Berlin Heidelberg New York |page=iii}}</ref> [[David Gieseker]] later distinguished, for step #2, going via [[Torelli's theorem]], which was Mumford's original method, and the alternative approach via the [[Chow point]] of a curve ''C'', in its projective [[canonical bundle#General case|canonical embedding]], which proves the [[stability (algebraic geometry)|stability]] of this point.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mumford |first1=David |title=Selected Papers: On the Classification of Varieties and Moduli Spaces |date=15 July 2004 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-387-21092-6 |page=3 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=df_X80mKSi0C&pg=PA3 |language=en}}</ref>

The concept of [[stable vector bundle]] from moduli theory has been consequential in mathematical physics: "This is a mathematical notion of stability, but it also corresponds to physical stability, at least in a regime in which quantum corrections are small."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Francoise |first1=Jean-Pierre |last2=Naber |first2=Gregory L. |last3=Tsun |first3=Tsou Sheung |title=Encyclopedia of Mathematical Physics |date=20 June 2006 |publisher=Elsevier Science |isbn=978-0-12-512660-1 |page=45 |language=en}}</ref>

====Moduli stacks====
{{main|moduli stack}}

Before the mathematical concept of [[stack (mathematics)|stack]] had been defined, Mumford gave a detailed treatment of the [[moduli stack of elliptic curves]], in his paper ''Picard Groups of Moduli Problems''. In it, he made a calculation of (the analogue of) the stack's [[Picard group]].<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Schilling |editor-first=O. F. G. |editor-link=Otto Schilling |title=Arithmetical Algebraic Geometry. Proceedings Conference Purdue University, 1963 |date=1965 |publisher=Harper and Row |language=en}}</ref> Hartshorne wrote that, in the paper, Mumford

<blockquote>[...] makes the point that to investigate the more subtle properties of curves, the [[coarse moduli space]] may not carry enough information, and so one should really work with stacks.<ref name="Hartshorne"/></blockquote>

===Classification of surfaces===
{{details|Enriques–Kodaira classification#Classification in positive characteristic}}
In three papers written between 1969 and 1976 (the last two in collaboration with [[Enrico Bombieri]]), Mumford extended the [[Enriques–Kodaira classification]] of smooth [[projective surface]]s from the case of the complex [[ground field]] to the case of an [[algebraically closed]] ground field of characteristic ''p''. The four classes are:<ref>{{Citation |last=Mumford |first=David |title=Global Analysis (Papers in Honor of K. Kodaira) |pages=325–339 |year=1969 |chapter=Enriques' classification of surfaces in char p I |location=Tokyo |publisher=Univ. Tokyo Press |doi=10.1515/9781400871230-019 |isbn=978-1-4008-7123-0 |jstor=j.ctt13x10qw.21 |mr=0254053 |author-link=David Mumford}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Bombieri |first1=Enrico |title=Complex analysis and algebraic geometry |pages=23–42 |year=1977 |chapter=Enriques' classification of surfaces in char. p. II |location=Tokyo |publisher=Iwanami Shoten |mr=0491719 |last2=Mumford |first2=David |author1-link=Enrico Bombieri |author2-link=David Mumford}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Bombieri |first1=Enrico |title=Enriques' classification of surfaces in char. p. III. |journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]] |volume=35 |pages=197–232 |year=1976 |url=https://dash.harvard.edu/bitstream/1/3612776/3/Mumford_EnriquesClassIII.pdf |bibcode=1976InMat..35..197B |doi=10.1007/BF01390138 |mr=0491720 |s2cid=122816845 |last2=Mumford |first2=David |author1-link=Enrico Bombieri |author2-link=David Mumford}}</ref>

# Kodaira dimension minus infinity.  These are the [[ruled surface]]s.
# Kodaira dimension 0.  These are the [[K3 surface]]s, [[abelian surface]]s, hyperelliptic and [[quasi-hyperelliptic surface]]s, and [[Enriques surface]]s.  There are classical and non-classical examples in the last two Kodaira dimension zero cases.
# Kodaira dimension 1. These are the elliptic and [[quasi-elliptic surface]]s not contained in the last two groups.
# Kodaira dimension 2. These are the [[surfaces of general type]].

===Explicit equations and algebraic techniques===
Mumford wrote on an algebraic approach to the classical theory of [[theta function]]s, the [[theta representation]], showing that its algebraic content was large, with resulting finite analogues of the [[Heisenberg group]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mumford |first1=David |title=Selected Papers: On the Classification of Varieties and Moduli Spaces |date=15 July 2004 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-387-21092-6 |page=293 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=df_X80mKSi0C&pg=PA293 |language=en}}</ref> This work on the [[equations defining abelian varieties]] appeared in 1966–7. He also is one of the founders of the [[Toric geometry|toroidal embedding]] theory, the geometric approach to varieties defined by [[monomial]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kempf |first1=G. |last2=Knudsen |first2=F. |last3=Mumford |first3=D. |last4=Saint-Donat |first4=B. |title=Toroidal Embeddings I |series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |date=1973 |volume=339 |doi=10.1007/BFb0070318 |isbn=978-3-540-06432-9 |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/BFb0070318 |language=en}}</ref> With [[Dave Bayer]] he published a paper "What can be computed in algebraic geometry?" in 1993 on computation and algebraic geometry, in which [[Gröbner basis]] techniques are fundamental.<ref>{{cite book |editor-last1=Eisenbud |editor-first1=David |editor-last2=Robbiano |editor-first2=Lorenzo |title=Computational Algebraic Geometry and Commutative Algebra: Cortona 1991 | series = Symposia mathematica |date=1993 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=1–48 |language=en}}</ref> The concept of [[Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity]] has been employed as a complexity measure for Gröbner bases.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Seiler |first1=Werner M. |title=Involution: The Formal Theory of Differential Equations and its Applications in Computer Algebra |date=26 October 2009 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-642-01287-7 |page=232 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YERK5ptJd9QC&pg=PA232 |language=en}}</ref>

===Vision===
{{main|computer vision}}

In a paper published in 1989, Mumford and Jayant Shah showed that a numerical method could tackle [[image segmentation]], using what became known as the [[Mumford–Shah functional]]. In the ''Handbook of Mathematical Methods in Imaging'' (2011) the functional was called "classical", and the method described as an [[energy minimization]] approach allowing optimal computation for [[piecewise function]] solutions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mumford |first1=David |last2=Shah |first2=Jayant |title=Optimal approximations by piecewise smooth functions and associated variational problems |journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics |date=July 1989 |volume=42 |issue=5 |pages=577–685 |doi=10.1002/cpa.3160420503}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |editor-last1=Scherzer |editor-first1=Otmar |title=Handbook of Mathematical Methods in Imaging |date=23 November 2010 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-387-92919-4 |page=1097 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FzvNfkMjvPwC&pg=PA1097 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Montegranario |first1=Hebert |title=An Introduction to Variational Calculus: Applications in Image Processing |date=23 December 2024 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-031-77270-2 |page=127 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LyM6EQAAQBAJ&pg=PA127 |language=en}}</ref> Another assessment in 2024 was "a foundational approach for partitioning an image into meaningful regions while preserving edges."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Montegranario |first1=Hebert |title=An Introduction to Variational Calculus: Applications in Image Processing |date=23 December 2024 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-031-77270-2 |page=127 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LyM6EQAAQBAJ&pg=PA127 |language=en}}</ref>

Following work of [[Shimon Ullman]] who brought in variational methods, and [[Berthold K.P. Horn]], Mumford in 1992 addressed the [[amodal completion]] problem with concepts from [[elastica theory]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Petitot |first1=Jean |title=Neurogeometry of V1 and Kanizsa Contours |journal=Axiomathes |date=September 2003 |volume=13 |issue=3–4 |pages=347–363 |doi=10.1023/B:AXIO.0000007240.49326.7e}}</ref> In the 1990s, [[Song-Chun Zhu]] at the [[University of Science and Technology of China]], attracted into the field by the book ''Vision'' (1982) by [[David Marr (scientist)|David Marr]], studied computer science under Mumford.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zhu |first1=Song-Chun |last2=Wu |first2=Ying Nian |title=Computer Vision: Statistical Models for Marr's Paradigm |date=15 March 2023 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-96530-3 |page=xiii |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=BSa0EAAAQBAJ&pg=PR13 |language=en}}</ref>

In 2002, Mumford and Tai Sing Lee proposed a model for the [[visual cortex]], influenced by work on [[pattern theory]] by [[Ulf Grenander]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=TS |last2=Mumford |first2=D |title=Hierarchical Bayesian inference in the visual cortex. |journal=Journal of the Optical Society of America. A, Optics, image science, and vision |date=July 2003 |volume=20 |issue=7 |pages=1434-48 |doi=10.1364/josaa.20.001434 |pmid=12868647}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Nilsson |first1=Nils J. |title=The Quest for Artificial Intelligence |date=30 October 2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-139-64282-8 |page=480 |url=https://www.google.co.uk/books?id=nUJdAAAAQBAJ&pg=PT480 |language=en}}</ref> The book chapter "The Evolving Concept of Cortical Hierarchy" from 2023 by Vezoli, Hou and Kennedy states that Mumford's "[[Bayesian]] computational approach to cortical hierarchy was revolutionary".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vezoli |first1=Julien |last2=Hou |first2=Yujie |last3=Kennedy |first3=Henry |title=The Evolving Concept of Cortical Hierarchy |journal=The Cerebral Cortex and Thalamus |date=December 2023 |pages=401 |doi=10.1093/med/9780197676158.003.0037 |url=https://www.google.com/books?id=pMrfEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA401}}</ref> The 2023 book by Zhu and Wu, ''Computer Vision: Statistical Models for Marr's Paradigm'', in its Preface lists as "pioneers of vision" [[Béla Julesz]] and [[King-Sun Fu]], with Grenander, Maar and Mumford.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zhu |first1=Song-Chun |last2=Wu |first2=Ying Nian |title=Computer Vision: Statistical Models for Marr's Paradigm |date=15 March 2023 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-030-96530-3 |url=https://www.google.com/books?id=BSa0EAAAQBAJ&pg=PR5 |page=v |language=en}}</ref>

==Promulgation of the ideas of Alexander Grothendieck==
In 1962 Mumford was appointed an assistant professor at Harvard.<ref name="Agarwal">{{cite book |last1=Agarwal |first1=Ravi P. |title=IMU, ICM, Medals, Prizes, and Laureates |date=19 October 2025 |publisher=MDPI |isbn=978-3-7258-4616-0 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XOKZEQAAQBAJ&pg=PA56 |language=en}}</ref> He decided to give a lecture course on a topic in the area of curves on an [[algebraic surface]], to illustrate the importance of the innovative approach in algebraic geometry of [[Alexander Grothendieck]], based at [[IHES]] near Paris.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Parikh |first1=Carol |title=The Unreal Life of Oscar Zariski |date=23 December 2008 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-387-09430-4 |page=117 note 153 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7u1HMMGNv60C&pg=PA117 |language=en}}</ref> The class notes of this course, given 1963–4, were published in 1966 as ''Lectures on Curves on an Algebraic Surface'', and in the Introduction Mumford wrote that the goal was to give an exposition of a "[[corollary]]" in [[Séminaire Nicolas Bourbaki (1960–1969)|Bourbaki seminar #221]] given by Grothendieck in early 1961, ''Techniques de construction et théorèmes d'existence en géométrie algébrique. IV : Les schémas de Hilbert'', in the [[TDTE]] series. It related to a vexed question in the legacy of the [[Italian school of algebraic geometry]], called the "completeness of the characteristic system" of a suitable algebraic system of curves. The issue was of a possible "[[pathological (mathematics)|pathology]]", and the burden of the course was to show that a [[necessary and sufficient condition]] for the validity of the theorem was now available.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mumford |first1=David |title=Lectures on Curves on an Algebraic Surface |date=2 March 2016 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-1-4008-8206-9 |pages=vii-viii |language=en}}</ref> In parallel, [[Robin Hartshorne]] was leading a seminar at Harvard, "Residues and Duality", on [[coherent duality]] in Grothendieck's [[derived category]] setting, in which Mumford, Tate, [[Stephen Lichtenbaum]] and others participated.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hartshorne |first1=Robin |title=Residues and Duality: Lecture Notes of a Seminar on the Work of A. Grothendieck, Given at Harvard 1963 /64 |date=14 November 2006 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-34794-1 |page=5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VgV8CwAAQBAJ&pg=PP5 |language=en}}</ref>

===''The Red Book''===
Mumford's lecture notes on [[scheme theory]] circulated for years in unpublished form. A geometric motivation for the theory brought forward by Mumford was "[[infinitesimals]] well adapted to algebraic and geometric structures."<ref>{{cite book |title=Bulletin of the Belgian Mathematical Society, Simon Stevin |date=2006 |publisher=Société mathématique de Belgique |page=1033|volume=13|issue=5 |language=en}}</ref> In 1979 in the ''[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]]'' a reviewer wrote of this work that it "initiated a generation of students to the subject when nothing else was available."<ref>{{cite book |title=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |date=1979 |publisher=Society |page=513|volume=1 (new series) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KCsRAQAAMAAJ |language=en}}</ref> At the time, they were, beside the treatise ''[[Éléments de géométrie algébrique]]'', the only accessible introduction.

Starting in 1967, the notes were mimeographed, bound in red cardboard, and distributed by Harvard's mathematics department under the title ''Introduction to Algebraic Geometry (Preliminary version of first 3 Chapters)''. Later (1988; 1999, 2nd ed., {{isbn|3-540-63293-X}}), they were published by Springer under the [[Lecture Notes in Mathematics]] series as ''The Red Book of Varieties and Schemes''. In an introduction to the 1988 edition, Mumford wrote

<blockquote>[...] Grothendieck came along and turned a confused world of researchers upside down, overwhelming them with the new terminology of schemes as well as with a huge production of new and very exciting results. These notes attempted to show something that was still very controversial at that time: that schemes really were the most natural language for algebraic geometry [...]<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mumford |first1=David |title=The Red Book of Varieties and Schemes |date=11 November 2013 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-662-21581-4 |page=iv |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q83yCAAAQBAJ&pg=PR4 |language=en}}</ref></blockquote>

===Grothendieck's relative point of view===
{{main|Grothendieck's relative point of view}}

In ''Lectures on Curves on an Algebraic Surface'', Mumford wrote "by far the most important categorical notion for algebraic geometry is that of [[fibre product]]."<ref>''Lectures on Curves on an Algebraic Surface'', p.21.</ref> Lectures 3 and 4 (with its Appendix on the [[Zariski tangent space]]) were a concise introduction to the circle of ideas, based on scheme theory (the book uses the older terminology of pre-schemes) known as [[Grothendieck's relative point of view]], with geometric illustrations. The [[representable functor]] point of view is central: Mumford illustrates it by citing contemporary research: [[Brown's representability theorem]] in [[homotopy theory]], where representable functors are clearly distinguished; Tate's [[rigid analytic space]]s; [[Jaap Murre]]'s work on functors to the [[category of groups]]; and [[Teruhisa Matsusaka]]'s theory of Q-varieties as an extension of the functors considered.<ref name="Lectures18">''Lectures on Curves on an Algebraic Surface'', p.18.</ref>

Grothendieck made a case for the "representable functor" approach to replace the [[universal object]] conceptualization then prevalent in [[category theory]]. For moduli spaces, the classical idea of a "universal family of curves" would therefore be modified to a functor "of curves", with a proof that it was representable. The satisfactory picture from homotopy theory, of a [[universal bundle]] with base space a [[classifying space]] that represents bundles does not, however, apply directly to moduli. Hence the distinction between a "coarse moduli space", via its [[geometric point]]s a universal object, and a [[fine moduli space]] which represents a functor of all parametrized families of curves. The latter is in line with the "relative point of view". In ''Geometric Invariant Theory'' Mumford laid out the issues for moduli theory, stating that currently "one knows very few ways in which to pose a plausible fine moduli problem." He went on to state that in technical terms the fine moduli problem was not "essentially harder", given "descent machinery", a reference to the role [[descent morphism]]s play.<ref>''Geometric Invariant Theory'', pp. 96–97.</ref>

This background explains why [[faithfully flat descent]] is introduced in Lecture 4 of ''Lectures on Curves on an Algebraic Surface'': as a necessary condition for representability of a functor. Mumford names the representability issue for schemes "Grothendieck's existence problem", a nod to [[Riemann's existence theorem]] and to Grothendieck's existence theorem for [[formal scheme]]s.<ref name="Lectures18"/> Mumford's remark about fibre products may be unpacked in later terms of [[Grothendieck fibration]]s and [[descent theory]].<ref>{{nLab|id=Grothendieck+fibration|title=Grothendieck fibration}}</ref><ref>{{nLab|id=descent|title=descent}}</ref> He went much further into the relative theory, in defining "modular families" of curves via [[Grothendieck topologies]], in ''Picard Groups of Moduli Problems''.<ref>''Picard Groups of Moduli Problems'', p. 52.</ref>

The lacuna of the mid-1960s theory in terms of sufficient conditions for representability of functors, as would apply to moduli problems, was filled through work of [[Michael Artin]] and others by 1969. There were two sides to this advance. (1) Further innovation in the foundations came with [[algebraic space]]s (more general than schemes but more restricted than Matsusaka's Q-varieties or Mumford's stacks). Algebraic spaces allow more quotients by equivalence relations than schemes. (2) This definition was combined with a thorough use of algebraic infinitesimal techniques around [[artinian ring]]s (commutative and [[local ring|local]]). See [[Artin's criterion]], [[formal moduli]], [[Schlessinger's theorem]].<ref>{{nLab|id=Artin+representability theorem|title=Artin representability+theorem}}</ref><ref>Michael Artin, Algebraization of formal moduli. I, ''Global Analysis (Papers in Honor of K. Kodaira)'', Princeton Univ. Press, Princeton, N.J., 1969, pp. 21-71. MR0260746 (41:5369)</ref>

==Awards and honors==
[[File:Mumford2.jpg|thumb|220px|David Mumford in 1975]]
Mumford was awarded a [[Fields Medal]] in 1974.  He was a
[[MacArthur Fellow]] from 1987 to 1992. He won the [[Shaw Prize]] in 2006.  In 2007 he was awarded the [[Steele Prize]] for Mathematical Exposition by the [[American Mathematical Society]]. In 2008 he was awarded the [[Wolf Prize]];<ref name=mt>{{MacTutor Biography|id=Mumford}}</ref> on receiving the prize in Jerusalem from [[Shimon Peres]], Mumford announced that he was donating half of the prize money to [[Birzeit University]] in the [[Palestinian territories]] and half to [[Gisha (human rights organization)|Gisha]], an Israeli human rights organization.<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.haaretz.com/1.4984908|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181123065627/https://www.haaretz.com/1.4984908|url-status=dead|archive-date=23 November 2018|title=U.S. prof. gives Israeli prize money to Palestinian university – Haaretz – Israel News|publisher=[[Haaretz]]|date=2008-05-26 |access-date=2008-05-26}}</ref><ref name=notices-ams>{{citation|last=Mumford|first=David|title=The Wolf Prize and Supporting Palestinian Education|journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society|date=September 2008|volume=55|issue=8|pages=919|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200808/200808-full-issue.pdf|publisher=American Mathematical Society|issn=0002-9920}}</ref> In 2010 he was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]].<ref>{{citation|url=https://news.brown.edu/pressreleases/2010/10/mumford|title=Mathematician David Mumford to receive National Medal of Science|publisher=[[Brown University]]|date=2010-10-15|access-date=2010-10-25}}</ref> In 2012 he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-02-10.</ref>

Further awards and honors include:

*Elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 1975.<ref name=mt/>
*Honorary Fellow from [[Tata Institute of Fundamental Research]] in 1978.<ref name=mt/>
*Honorary D.Sc. from the [[University of Warwick]] in 1983.<ref name=mt/>
*Foreign Member of [[Accademia dei Lincei|Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei]], [[Rome]], in 1991.<ref name=mt/>
*Honorary Member of [[London Mathematical Society]] in 1995.<ref name=mt/>
*Elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 1997.<ref>{{citation|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=David+Mumford&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-12-08|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref>
*Honorary D.Sc. from [[Norwegian University of Science and Technology]] in 2000.<ref>[https://www.ntnu.edu/phd/honorary-doctors NTNU's list of honorary doctors]</ref>
*Honorary D.Sc. from [[Rockefeller University]] in 2001.<ref name=mt/>
*[[Longuet-Higgins Prize]] in 2005 and 2009.
*Honorary Doctorate from [[Chennai Mathematical Institute]] in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chennai Mathematical Institute |url=https://www.cmi.ac.in//events/honoriscausa.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100122171806/https://www.cmi.ac.in//events/honoriscausa.php |archive-date=2010-01-22 |access-date=2025-07-07 |website=www.cmi.ac.in}}</ref>
*Foreign Member of [[The Royal Society]] in 2008.<ref name=mt/>
*Foreign Member of the [[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]].<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40116 |title=Gruppe 1: Matematiske fag |publisher=[[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]] |language=no |access-date=7 October 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131110152102/http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40116 |archive-date=10 November 2013 }}</ref>
*Honorary Doctorate from [[Brown University]] in 2011.<ref>{{citation|url = http://www.browndailyherald.com/commencement-2011-honorary-degrees-1.2579444|title = Commencement 2011: Honorary degrees|date = 2011-05-29|access-date = 29 May 2011|archive-date = 15 March 2012|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120315122226/http://www.browndailyherald.com/commencement-2011-honorary-degrees-1.2579444|url-status = dead}}</ref>
*2012 [[BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Awards|BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award]] in the Basic Sciences category (jointly with Ingrid Daubechies).

Mumford was elected President of the [[International Mathematical Union]] in 1995 and served from 1995 to 1999.<ref name=mt/>
